sections.title: A cave that still shines
sections.intro_md:
Walk into the Lomas Rishi cave in the Barabar Hills, 35 km north of Gaya, and clap once. The sound rolls around a chamber cut into solid granite about 2,250 years ago and polished so smoothly that the walls still throw back the light of a torch. Masons working for the Maurya emperors made it. Their capital, Pataliputra, is now Patna.

That is Bihar's paradox in one room. This strip of the Ganga plain gave India its first great empires, the Buddha's enlightenment, the Jain teacher Mahavira, the mathematician Aryabhata, a monastery-university that drew scholars from China, and the word *vihara* (monastery) that became the state's own name.

Today Bihar has the lowest income per person of any Indian state, about a third of the national average, and had the lowest literacy in the 2011 census. It has also grown faster than India for three years running.

Both stories are true. Today is about how the same land produced both.

sections.title: Bihar in one page
sections.intro_md:
Bihar sits in eastern India, landlocked, with Nepal to the north, Uttar Pradesh to the west, West Bengal to the east and Jharkhand to the south. The Ganga flows west to east through the middle and splits it in two. **North Bihar** (Mithila, Champaran, the Kosi country) is flat, wet, fertile and floods most years. **South Bihar** (Magadh, Bhojpur, the hills of Rajgir and Gaya) is drier and rises toward the old plateau.

It became a province of its own on **22 March 1912**, carved out of the Bengal Presidency; that day is now Bihar Diwas. Orissa was separated in 1936. On **15 November 2000** the southern plateau became Jharkhand and took most of the state's coal, iron ore, forests and factories with it.

Hindi is the official language and Urdu the second official language, but at home most people speak **Bhojpuri, Maithili, Magahi, Angika or Bajjika**. Patna is the capital. There are 38 districts, 40 Lok Sabha seats and a 243-seat assembly.

sections.title: The land: rivers that move
sections.intro_md:
Almost all of Bihar is the floor of the Ganga valley: deep, soft alluvium laid down by rivers. That is why it is so fertile and so crowded. North of the Ganga, a row of Himalayan rivers (Ghaghara, Gandak, Burhi Gandak, Bagmati, Kamla, Kosi, Mahananda) run down to it, swollen by snowmelt and the monsoon at the same time. Most of north Bihar floods in a normal year, and a wet year can drown whole districts.

South of the Ganga the land is drier. The Son, Punpun and Phalgu come up from the plateau, and the old rocky hills of Rajgir, Barabar and Gaya poke out of the plain. In the far southwest the Kaimur plateau stands up like a wall.

Bihar lost most of its forests when Jharkhand was created in 2000. What is left is a thin rim: Valmiki in the north, Kaimur in the southwest, and wetlands like Kanwar Lake. The pins on the map below are the places this day keeps coming back to.

spotlights.name: The Ganga at Patna
spotlights.spot_it: A river so wide at Patna that the far bank is a grey line, crossed by a 5.6 km bridge on dozens of piers.
spotlights.story_md: Patna is a long, thin city: it runs for about 20 km along the south bank of the Ganga and barely 5 km inland, because the river decided its shape. Just upstream the **Son**, the **Gandak** and the **Ghaghara** all pour in, so by Patna the Ganga carries the water of half the Himalaya. **Mahatma Gandhi Setu**, opened in 1982, crosses it on 46 spans of about 121 m each, 5.575 km in all, and was long India's longest river bridge. Its sagging concrete deck was replaced with steel over 2017 to 2022. A rail and road bridge from Digha to Sonpur opened in 2016.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The river is Bihar's spine: every capital from Pataliputra to Patna sat on it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Patna is a city 20 km long and 5 km wide because the Ganga drew it.

spotlights.name: The Kosi, sorrow of Bihar
spotlights.spot_it: A braided river of sand bars and shifting channels, held between earth embankments that it keeps breaking.
spotlights.story_md: The Kosi drains Everest and Kanchenjunga, then drops onto the plains carrying one of the heaviest silt loads of any river on earth. It dumps that silt, raises its own bed, and jumps sideways. Over roughly 250 years it wandered about **120 km westward** across north Bihar. Engineers boxed it in with embankments from the 1950s and a barrage at Bhimnagar, just inside Nepal, in 1963. On **18 August 2008** the eastern embankment broke at Kusaha, 12 km upstream of the barrage. The river swung back about 120 km east into a channel it had left a century earlier and flooded districts that had forgotten it. Estimates of people affected run from 2.7 to 3.3 million.
spotlights.why_it_matters: North Bihar's floods are not bad luck; they are what a river like this does.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Kosi does not overflow. It moves house.

spotlights.name: Valmiki Tiger Reserve
spotlights.spot_it: Sal forest and grass at the foot of the Himalaya, where Bihar touches Nepal's Chitwan.
spotlights.story_md: Bihar's only tiger reserve fills the northwest tip of West Champaran, where the Shivalik hills rise out of the plain. It is part of one forest that runs across the border into Chitwan National Park in Nepal, so tigers, rhinos and leopards cross without passports. The Gandak enters India here at Valmikinagar, where a barrage diverts it into canals. Local tradition says the sage Valmiki had his ashram in these hills, which is how the reserve and the town got their names. For a state that is under 8% forest, this is the one large wild block left.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that a crowded farming state can still hold tigers.
spotlights.memory_hook: In the most crowded state, tigers walk to Nepal and back.

spotlights.name: Ganges river dolphin
spotlights.spot_it: A grey dolphin with a long thin beak, rolling up for air with a puff, in muddy river water.
spotlights.story_md: The Ganges river dolphin is almost blind: its eyes have no lens and it hunts by echolocation in water too muddy to see through. Locals call it **susu**, after the sound of its breath. Since 1991 a 50 km stretch of the Ganga between Sultanganj and Kahalgaon in Bhagalpur district has been the **Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary**, the only protected area in India made for this animal. India declared it the national aquatic animal in 2009. Bihar holds a large share of the surviving population, because its stretch of the Ganga still flows deep and free between barrages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A top predator that only survives where the river is still a river.
spotlights.memory_hook: Blind, beaked, and named for the sound it makes: susu.

sections.title: Where Indian empire began
sections.intro_md:
Around 500 BCE north India was split into sixteen big states, the mahajanapadas. Two of them were in today's Bihar: **Magadha**, a monarchy south of the Ganga, and the **Vajji** league to the north, run by an assembly. Magadha won. It had iron from the hills to the south, elephants from the forests, rich rice land, and rivers for moving armies and grain.

Its kings moved the capital from the hill fortress of Rajagriha to Pataliputra on the Ganga. From there the **Nandas**, then the **Mauryas** (about 321 to 185 BCE) and later the **Guptas** (about 320 to 550 CE) ruled most of the subcontinent. In this one region the Buddha taught, Mahavira taught, Ashoka carved his edicts and Aryabhata did his astronomy.

How do we know? From Buddhist and Jain texts, from Greek writers such as Megasthenes, from Ashoka's own inscriptions, and from archaeology at Kumhrar, Vaishali, Rajgir and Nalanda. The timeline below runs from Magadha to the 2026 government.

spotlights.name: Rajagriha, the first capital
spotlights.spot_it: A ring of five rocky hills with a dry-stone wall snaking along the ridges.
spotlights.story_md: Before Patna there was **Rajagriha**, today's Rajgir: a valley ringed by five hills that made a natural fortress. King **Bimbisara** of Magadha ruled from here in the Buddha's lifetime, and his son **Ajatashatru** is said to have imprisoned him and seized the throne. The **Cyclopean Wall**, built of huge undressed stones fitted without mortar, once ran about 40 km along the ridges and is among the oldest stone fortifications in India. The Buddha taught often on **Gridhakuta**, Vulture's Peak, and tradition places the first Buddhist council in a cave here soon after his death.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Magadha's rise to empire began in this hill fort.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five hills, one wall, and a king locked up by his own son.

spotlights.name: Vaishali, a republic of 2,500 years ago
spotlights.spot_it: A single polished pillar crowned by a lion, beside a brick stupa in green fields.
spotlights.story_md: Vaishali was the capital of the **Licchavis**, leaders of the **Vajji league**, which was run not by a king but by an assembly of clan heads who met, debated and voted. Buddhist texts put the number of its rajas at 7,707, which is probably a story-teller's number but captures the idea. That makes it one of the earliest known republics anywhere. The Buddha visited often; the courtesan **Amrapali** gave him a mango grove here. Jains believe **Mahavira** was born at Kundagrama on its edge. Ashoka later raised a pillar at Kolhua topped by a single lion, still standing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A reminder that government by assembly has very old roots in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Vaishali voted while most of the world crowned kings.

spotlights.name: Pataliputra
spotlights.spot_it: A lone polished sandstone column in a Patna park: all that stands of a Mauryan hall of 80 pillars.
spotlights.story_md: Ajatashatru built a fort at the village of Pataligrama where the Son met the Ganga. Under **Chandragupta Maurya** (from about 321 BCE) it became the capital of an empire. The Greek envoy **Megasthenes**, who lived here around 300 BCE, described a city about 15 km long behind a wooden wall with **570 towers and 64 gates**. In 1912 to 1913 excavators at **Kumhrar** in Patna found the remains of a hall of 80 polished sandstone pillars. Tradition credits **Chanakya**, Chandragupta's minister, with the *Arthashastra*, a hard-headed manual on statecraft, though scholars think the text grew over centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: For about 800 years, under Mauryas and Guptas, this was the capital of most of India.
spotlights.memory_hook: 570 towers, 64 gates, and one column left standing.

spotlights.name: Ashoka
spotlights.spot_it: Emperor's pillars in Bihar: smooth stone columns with a lion or bull on top, standing in open fields.
spotlights.story_md: Ashoka was born in Pataliputra around 304 BCE and ruled from it. After his bloody conquest of Kalinga (Odisha) around 261 BCE he turned to Buddhism and had moral messages carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, in the first large body of writing India has left us. Bihar holds some of the best-preserved pillars. At **Lauriya Nandangarh** in West Champaran a 12 m column still stands with its lion on top, much as it was raised. At **Rampurva** two pillars were found; the bull capital now stands in Rashtrapati Bhavan. India's national emblem, though, is the lion capital from Sarnath in Uttar Pradesh.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ashoka's edicts are where Indian written history really begins.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born in Patna, remembered in stone across India.

spotlights.name: Barabar caves
spotlights.spot_it: A doorway in bare granite carved to look like a wooden hut, with a frieze of elephants; inside, walls polished like glass.
spotlights.story_md: In the Barabar Hills, workmen of the Maurya emperors carved artificial caves into solid granite and polished the insides to a mirror finish, with no gap between wall and ceiling. Inscriptions dedicate them to the **Ajivikas**, a sect of ascetics who believed everything is fixed by fate (see today's side dish). The **Lomas Rishi** cave copies a timber and thatch hut in stone, curved eaves and all; it is the earliest surviving example of the arch shape that later fronted Ajanta and Karla. The caves are India's oldest surviving rock-cut chambers, though the Son Bhandar caves at Rajgir may be older. E. M. Forster turned them into the Marabar Caves of *A Passage to India*.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The start of India's 1,000-year tradition of carving temples out of rock.
spotlights.memory_hook: Granite polished like glass, then lent to a novel as the Marabar Caves.

compare.difference: Son Bhandar is rougher and may be slightly older. Barabar has the famous mirror polish and the carved hut-shaped doorway.

spotlights.name: Aryabhata
spotlights.spot_it: A scholar of Kusumapura (Patna) who wrote, in 499 CE, that the earth spins.
spotlights.story_md: Aryabhata wrote the *Aryabhatiya* in 499 CE, when, he tells us, he was 23 years old, and he worked at **Kusumapura**, generally identified with Pataliputra. In 121 short verses he gives pi as 62,832 divided by 20,000, that is 3.1416, correct to four decimal places. He says the earth turns on its axis and that the stars only appear to move, like the bank seen from a moving boat. He explains eclipses with shadows, not demons. India named its first satellite after him in 1975. No ancient portrait survives; every statue of him is imagined.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the first mathematicians in the world to state that the earth rotates.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-three years old, 121 verses, pi to four decimals.

sections.title: Nalanda: the monastery the world came to
sections.intro_md:
For about 700 years, students from China, Korea, Tibet and Southeast Asia travelled for months to reach a cluster of brick monasteries in south Bihar. Nalanda was not a university in the modern sense; it was a Buddhist monastic community where teaching and debate were the daily work. But it had what we would recognise: entrance tests, famous teachers, a vast library and a reputation that crossed oceans.

Around it the Pala kings (8th to 12th centuries) founded more monasteries: **Vikramashila**, **Odantapuri** (near today's Bihar Sharif) and others. Their teachers carried Indian Buddhism to Tibet, where it survives today.

Around 1200 these monasteries were sacked during raids by Turkic armies under **Bakhtiyar Khalji**. The popular story of a library burning for months comes from much later accounts. What we do know: a Tibetan pilgrim, Dharmasvamin, visited in the 1230s and found a few monks still teaching amid the ruins. Then Nalanda was forgotten until the 19th century. In 2024 a new Nalanda University opened its 455-acre, net-zero campus at Rajgir, 12 km from the ruins.

spotlights.name: Nalanda Mahavihara
spotlights.spot_it: Long red-brick monastery blocks of cells around courtyards, and a stepped stupa crowded with small votive stupas.
spotlights.story_md: Nalanda began as a Buddhist monastery under the Gupta kings in the 5th century and grew into the largest centre of learning in Asia. Monks studied Buddhist philosophy, but also logic, grammar, medicine and astronomy. Chinese visitors reported thousands of resident monks; their numbers vary, from about 3,000 to 10,000. Getting in was hard: the gatekeepers were scholars who questioned applicants, and, according to Xuanzang, most failed. Its library was called **Dharmaganja**, the mart of religion. The excavated part is only a fraction of the site; much still lies under nearby fields. UNESCO listed it in 2016.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The model for every later Buddhist university from Tibet to Indonesia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Even getting through the gate was an exam.

spotlights.name: Xuanzang
spotlights.spot_it: A Chinese monk walking with a frame of scrolls on his back.
spotlights.story_md: In 629 Xuanzang slipped out of China against an imperial ban and walked across the deserts of Central Asia to India, looking for the original texts of Buddhism. He spent years at Nalanda studying under its abbot **Shilabhadra**, and went home in 645 with hundreds of manuscripts. His travel record, *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, describes the monasteries, the debates and the daily routine. Twelve hundred years later the British archaeologist **Alexander Cunningham** used it like a guidebook to identify the ruins in 1861 to 1862. A memorial hall to him stands at Nalanda.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Much of what we know about Nalanda's daily life comes from his notes.
spotlights.memory_hook: A runaway monk wrote the map that found Nalanda again.

spotlights.name: Vikramashila
spotlights.spot_it: A huge cross-shaped brick stupa platform on a low mound near the Ganga.
spotlights.story_md: Around 800, the Pala king **Dharmapala** founded a second great monastery at Vikramashila, near today's Bhagalpur, as a rival to Nalanda. It became famous for tantric Buddhism and for its link with Tibet. Its best-known teacher, **Atisha Dipankara**, left for Tibet in the 1040s at the request of Tibetan kings and helped revive Buddhism there; Tibetans still revere him. Vikramashila was destroyed around 1200 in the same wave of raids that ended Nalanda. Its ruins were dug out only in the 1960s to 1980s, and a central university has been planned on a new campus nearby.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tibetan Buddhism runs partly through this site in Bihar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nalanda's younger rival sent its star teacher to Tibet.

sections.title: From Sher Shah to Jharkhand
sections.intro_md:
After the Guptas, Pataliputra faded and the political centre of India moved west. Bihar became a rich province ruled from elsewhere: by Delhi sultans, by the Afghan **Sher Shah Suri** (who was from Sasaram), by the Mughals, and by the Nawabs of Bengal.

In 1764 the East India Company won at **Buxar** and with it the right to tax Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Bihar's peasants grew the Company's opium, saltpetre and indigo. The famine of 1770 and the permanent land settlement of 1793 left a pattern of big landlords and poor tenants that shaped Bihar for two centuries.

Resistance came in waves: **Kunwar Singh** in 1857, Gandhi's **Champaran** satyagraha in 1917, and the Quit India rising of 1942, which was fiercest in Bihar and eastern UP. Bihar became its own province in 1912, gave India its first President in 1950, and in 1974 produced **JP's** movement against Indira Gandhi.

In 2000 the southern plateau left to become Jharkhand. Bihar kept the people and the floods; Jharkhand got most of the minerals.

spotlights.name: Sher Shah Suri
spotlights.spot_it: A colossal domed tomb of grey-red sandstone standing in the middle of a square lake at Sasaram.
spotlights.story_md: Farid Khan grew up on his father's estate at **Sasaram**; the name Sher Khan, legend says, came from killing a tiger. He beat the Mughal emperor **Humayun** at Chausa (1539, in today's Buxar district) and at Kannauj (1540) and drove him out of India. In just five years of rule he issued a silver coin of about 178 grains called the **rupiya**, the ancestor of the rupee, rebuilt the great road from Bengal to the northwest (later the Grand Trunk Road) with inns and wells, and organised a horse post. He died in 1545 in a gunpowder blast at Kalinjar fort. His tomb at Sasaram, about 37 m high, rises from an artificial lake.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The rupee and the Grand Trunk Road both trace back to a man from Sasaram.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Sasaram boy chased out the Mughals and named the rupee.

spotlights.name: The Battle of Buxar, 1764
spotlights.spot_it: An 18th-century British officer in red: Hector Munro, who won eastern India in one afternoon.
spotlights.story_md: On 22 October 1764 an East India Company army of about 7,000 under **Hector Munro** met the combined forces of Mir Qasim of Bengal, Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II near Buxar on the Ganga. The Company won. In 1765, by the Treaty of Allahabad, the emperor granted it the **diwani**, the right to collect revenue, of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. A trading company became the government of some 20 million people. Historians rank Buxar above the better-known Plassey (1757) as the battle that really made British rule.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where the Company stopped trading and started governing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Plassey opened the door; Buxar handed over the keys.

spotlights.name: Kunwar Singh
spotlights.spot_it: An old man with a long white beard: 'the Rebel of Arrah' as the Illustrated London News drew him in 1858.
spotlights.story_md: Kunwar Singh, the landowner of **Jagdispur** near Arrah, was about 80 when he joined the 1857 uprising. He led rebel sepoys in a campaign that ran from Bihar through central India and back, beating Company columns several times. The best-known story says that while crossing the Ganga a bullet hit his wrist, so he cut off his own arm with his sword and offered it to the river; it is a story, not a record. He retook Jagdispur on 23 April 1858 and died three days later. Bihar celebrates 23 April as his victory day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bihar's hero of 1857, and proof that the rebellion was not only a soldiers' mutiny.
spotlights.memory_hook: An 80-year-old rebel who, legend says, gave his arm to the Ganga.

spotlights.name: Golghar
spotlights.spot_it: A giant whitewashed beehive with an outside staircase that spirals to the top.
spotlights.story_md: After the famine of 1770, which killed millions in Bengal and Bihar, Governor-General Warren Hastings ordered granaries. Captain **John Garstin** built this one in Patna in 1786: a solid dome about 29 m high with walls several metres thick at the base and no pillars inside. Workers were meant to climb the **145 steps** of the outer stair, tip grain in through a hole at the top and walk down the other side. It was built to hold about 140,000 tonnes, but it was never filled. The popular explanation is that its doors opened inward, so a full granary could not be opened. Climb it for the best view of Patna and the Ganga.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A monument to famine, and to planning that did not quite work.
spotlights.memory_hook: A famine granary that was never filled.

spotlights.name: Champaran Satyagraha, 1917
spotlights.spot_it: Indigo country in West Champaran, where Gandhi ran his first satyagraha in India.
spotlights.story_md: Under the **tinkathia** system, peasants in Champaran had to grow indigo on 3 kathas of every 20 (three-twentieths of their land) for European planters, at prices the planters set. A farmer named **Raj Kumar Shukla** followed Gandhi around until he agreed to come. Gandhi arrived in April 1917; when the district ordered him to leave Motihari he refused and said he would accept the punishment. The case was dropped. Lawyers including **Rajendra Prasad** and **Anugrah Narayan Sinha** recorded thousands of peasants' statements. The Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918 abolished tinkathia.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first satyagraha in India: the method that would later win independence was tested in Bihar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three kathas in twenty, and one stubborn farmer who would not let Gandhi go.

spotlights.name: Jayaprakash Narayan (JP)
spotlights.spot_it: An old man in spectacles addressing a sea of people at Patna's Gandhi Maidan in 1974.
spotlights.story_md: Born in 1902 at **Sitab Diara** on the Bihar and UP border, JP studied in the United States for seven years, paying his way picking grapes and working in factories, and came back a socialist. In 1974 students in Bihar protested against corruption and prices; JP, then 71, took the lead and on 5 June 1974 at Gandhi Maidan called for **sampoorna kranti**, total revolution. The movement spread, Indira Gandhi declared the Emergency in 1975, and in 1977 the Janata Party threw her out. Lalu Prasad and Nitish Kumar, who would run Bihar for 35 years, both started as JP's student activists.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bihar's politics of the last 50 years grew out of his movement.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 71-year-old who brought down a prime minister, and raised two chief ministers.

sections.title: Four faiths, one small region
sections.intro_md:
Few regions on earth matter to so many religions at once. Within about 100 km of Gaya lie the place of the Buddha's enlightenment, the places of Mahavira's birth, teaching and death, the most important site in Hinduism for rites for the dead, and, in Patna, the birthplace of the tenth Sikh guru. Sufi shrines at Maner and Bihar Sharif add a fifth thread. Sitamarhi in the north is linked by tradition with the birth of Sita. The Bodhi Tree at Bodh Gaya is itself probably a descendant, via Sri Lanka, of the tree the Buddha sat under.

Bihar's population is about 82% Hindu and about 18% Muslim according to the 2023 caste survey. Buddhists and Jains are a tiny share of residents, but their pilgrims fill Bodh Gaya, Rajgir and Pawapuri every winter, many from Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Japan, Tibet and Bhutan.

Everyday faith is often less about temples than about rivers and the sun: Chhath, Bihar's biggest festival, has no priest and no idol (see Festivals).

spotlights.name: Mahabodhi Temple, Bodh Gaya
spotlights.spot_it: A tall straight-sided brick pyramid tower with four small corner towers, set in a sunken courtyard full of monks.
spotlights.story_md: This is where, Buddhists believe, Siddhartha sat under a pipal tree and became the Buddha. Ashoka built the first shrine here in the 3rd century BCE; the present tower, about 55 m tall, dates from the 5th to 6th centuries and is one of the oldest brick temples still standing in India. It was a ruin when the Burmese king sent a restoration mission in the 1870s; Alexander Cunningham's team finished the work in the 1880s. UNESCO listed it in 2002. Since 1949 a committee of Hindu and Buddhist members has managed it, an arrangement some Buddhist groups have long campaigned to change.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The holiest site in the Buddhist world, visited by pilgrims from every Buddhist country.
spotlights.memory_hook: One tree, one seat, one tower: the centre of the Buddhist world is in Gaya district.

spotlights.name: Vishnupad temple, Gaya
spotlights.spot_it: A grey stone temple on the bank of the Phalgu, packed in September with families making rice-ball offerings for their dead.
spotlights.story_md: Inside is a footprint about 40 cm long set in basalt, believed to be **Vishnu's**. The present temple was built in 1787 by **Ahilyabai Holkar**, the Maratha queen of Indore. Gaya's real importance is **pind daan**: Hindus believe that offering balls of rice and sesame here frees the souls of ancestors. During **Pitru Paksha**, the fortnight of the ancestors in September, lakhs of pilgrims come from across India and abroad, and hereditary priests called Gayawal pandas keep books recording which families have come, going back generations. The Phalgu next to the temple is dry sand for most of the year; you dig to find its water.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gaya is the Hindu world's main place for rites for the dead.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Gaya the dead have a waiting list, and the priests keep the ledgers.

spotlights.name: Takht Sri Patna Sahib
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble gurdwara with golden domes in the old city of Patna.
spotlights.story_md: **Guru Gobind Singh**, the tenth Sikh guru, was born here on 22 December 1666, while his father Guru Tegh Bahadur was travelling in Bengal and Assam. He spent his first years in Patna before the family moved to Punjab. The site is one of the **five takhts**, the seats of authority of the Sikh faith, and the only one in eastern India. Maharaja Ranjit Singh funded an earlier building; the present one was rebuilt after the 1934 earthquake. In 2017 Patna hosted the 350th anniversary of the guru's birth, with pilgrims housed in tent cities on Gandhi Maidan.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Why the Sikh faith has one of its five thrones on the Ganga.
spotlights.memory_hook: The guru of the Khalsa was a Patna-born boy.

spotlights.name: Jal Mandir, Pawapuri
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble temple floating in a lotus pond, reached by a 180 m causeway.
spotlights.story_md: Jains believe **Mahavira**, the 24th tirthankara, attained nirvana at Pawapuri; tradition dates it to 527 BCE, while many historians place it about a century later. The story goes that so many people came to take a pinch of earth from his cremation ground that they dug a pond, and the Jal Mandir now stands in the middle of it. Jains mark his nirvana at **Diwali**, so the lamps lit across India that night carry, for Jains, a meaning that begins here. Nearby Rajgir and Vaishali also belong to his story, which makes Bihar the land of Mahavira's life, teaching and death.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bihar is to Jainism what Bodh Gaya is to Buddhism.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple in a pond dug by a crowd taking pinches of earth.

spotlights.name: Mundeshwari temple
spotlights.spot_it: A small octagonal stone temple on a hilltop in Kaimur, with worship still going on inside.
spotlights.story_md: On Mundeshwari hill stands a small **octagonal** stone shrine, a rare plan for an Indian temple, with a four-faced Shiva linga and an image of the goddess. It is often called the oldest functioning Hindu temple in India, meaning worship has never stopped. How old is disputed. A sign at the site gives 108 CE; many scholars date the temple and its inscription to the 6th or 7th century. Either way it is among the earliest stone temples in north India. Goats offered to the goddess are not killed: the priest sprinkles rice on them and they are let go.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare survivor of the first age of Hindu stone temples.
spotlights.memory_hook: An eight-sided temple where the sacrificed goat walks home.

sections.title: Five languages under one label
sections.intro_md:
Officially Bihar speaks Hindi. At home it speaks something else. **Bhojpuri** is the language of the west (Bhojpur, Saran, Champaran) and of eastern UP; **Maithili** of the north (Mithila); **Magahi** of the south around Patna and Gaya; **Angika** around Bhagalpur; **Bajjika** around Muzaffarpur and Vaishali. They are related, but a Maithili speaker and a Bhojpuri speaker can find each other hard going. **Urdu** is the second official language and is spoken by many Muslims across the state.

Bhojpuri travelled furthest. From 1834, indentured labourers, the girmitiya, sailed from Calcutta to Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad, Guyana and Suriname, and a large share came from Bhojpuri districts. Bhojpuri survives today in Mauritius and in the chutney music of the Caribbean. At home, Bhojpuri cinema, born in 1963 with *Ganga Maiyya Tohe Piyari Chadhaibo*, is a large film industry.

Hindi literature owes Bihar a lot: **Ramdhari Singh Dinkar**, whose line "Singhasan khali karo ki janta aati hai" (vacate the throne, the people are coming) became JP's slogan, and **Phanishwar Nath Renu**, whose novel *Maila Anchal* put Purnia's villages into the Hindi canon.

spotlights.name: Maithili and the Tirhuta script
spotlights.spot_it: A script with hooked letters, cousin to Bengali, used for Maithili in Mithila.
spotlights.story_md: Maithili is the language of **Mithila**, the plains of north Bihar and Nepal's Terai. It has a literary history of 700 years and its own script, **Tirhuta** or Mithilakshar, a cousin of the Bengali and Odia scripts; most people now write it in Devanagari. In 2003 it was added to the **Eighth Schedule** of the Constitution. In Nepal it is the second most spoken language. Maithili speakers have campaigned for a separate Mithila state since the mid-20th century, and Tirhuta was added to Unicode in 2014.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows that 'Hindi-speaking Bihar' hides several full languages.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mithila has its own tongue, script and painted walls.

spotlights.name: Vidyapati
spotlights.spot_it: A seated poet's statue at Bisfi, Madhubani: the man who wrote Radha's longing in Maithili.
spotlights.story_md: Vidyapati (about 1352 to 1448) was a court poet of Mithila who wrote love songs of **Radha and Krishna** in Maithili. His songs travelled east and were taken up by Bengal's Vaishnava devotees; Chaitanya is said to have sung them. They shaped a literary language, Brajabuli, used for centuries afterwards. As a teenager, **Rabindranath Tagore** wrote poems imitating him under the pen name Bhanusimha. A Mithila legend says Shiva himself came to work as Vidyapati's servant, named Ugna. His songs are still sung at Maithili weddings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The poet who made a regional language a language of devotion across eastern India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tagore's first pen-name was a tribute to a Maithili poet.

spotlights.name: Bhikhari Thakur and Bidesia
spotlights.spot_it: Village theatre in Bhojpuri where a wife sings to a husband who has gone east to Calcutta for work, with men playing the women's parts.
spotlights.story_md: Bhikhari Thakur (1887 to 1971) was a barber from Qutubpur in Saran district who worked in Kharagpur and saw what migration did to families. He formed a troupe and wrote plays in **Bhojpuri**. The most famous, **Bidesia**, is about a young wife left behind when her husband goes to the city and finds another woman. *Beti Bechwa* attacked the selling of daughters into marriage with old men. His actors were men, women's roles included, in the style called launda naach. He has been called the Shakespeare of Bhojpuri. The word *bidesia*, one who has gone away, became the name for a whole genre of migrant songs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He put migration, Bihar's central experience, on stage a century ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bidesia: the play about the man who left, from the man who saw them leave.

sections.title: Painted walls, polished stone, a reed pipe
sections.intro_md:
Bihar's most famous art was made by women on mud walls: **Mithila painting**. Next to it are crafts from the same homes (sikki grass, sujni quilts embroidered from old saris) and a different painted tradition from Bhagalpur, **Manjusha**. Patna added two city arts: **Patna Kalam** watercolours and **tikuli**.

In stone, Bihar has the first great age of Indian sculpture: the polished Mauryan pillars, animals and the Didarganj Yakshi. The Pala workshops of Nalanda later cast bronze Buddhas that shaped art in Tibet, Nepal and Java.

In music, the region gave India the shehnai of **Bismillah Khan**, the dhrupad of the Darbhanga gharana, and the folk voice of **Sharda Sinha**. Its theatre is the Bhojpuri stage of Bhikhari Thakur; its dances include Jat-Jatin and Jhijhiya.

Watch the two clips under Madhubani. The best way to tell Mithila from Manjusha is to see them side by side, as below.

rows.mithila: Many bright colours, black double outlines
Every space filled, no empty ground
rows.manjusha: Bordered panels, like a comic strip
Always Bihula and the snake goddess
Temple-shaped boxes of jute and bamboo

spotlights.name: Madhubani (Mithila) painting
spotlights.spot_it: Every space filled; figures outlined twice in black; fish, peacocks, bamboo, lotus and gods; flat bright colours.
spotlights.story_md: For centuries women in Mithila painted the mud walls of their homes, above all the **kohbar ghar**, the room where a newly married couple spends its first nights, with gods, fish and bamboo for fertility. Outsiders saw almost none of it until the **1934 earthquake** knocked down walls and a British officer, **William Archer**, photographed the paintings. After the drought of 1966 to 1968, the All India Handicrafts Board sent the artist **Bhaskar Kulkarni** to encourage women to paint on paper for sale. Jagdamba Devi, Sita Devi, Ganga Devi and Baua Devi became famous; **Dulari Devi**, once a domestic worker, won the Padma Shri in 2021. It received a GI tag in 2007.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's best-known folk arts, made almost entirely by women.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born on bedroom walls, revealed by an earthquake, saved by a drought.

compare.difference: Madhubani fills every space with double-outlined figures in many colours. Manjusha uses only pink, green and yellow, in panels like a comic strip, and always tells the Bihula story with snakes.

spotlights.name: Manjusha art
spotlights.spot_it: Pink, green and yellow panels framed with borders like a comic strip, crowded with snakes, on temple-shaped boxes.
spotlights.story_md: In Bhagalpur, every August, people worship **Bishahari**, the snake goddess, and carry painted temple-shaped boxes called **manjusha**, made of jute, bamboo and paper. The paintings tell one story: **Bihula**, whose husband Bala was killed by a snakebite on their wedding night, floats on a raft with his body to the gods and wins his life back. The art uses three main colours, pink, green and yellow, and runs the story across panels with borders, which is why it is often called India's earliest comic strip. It nearly vanished; artist Chakravarty Devi kept it alive into the 21st century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A narrative art from Anga, older Bhagalpur, with its own visual grammar.
spotlights.memory_hook: A widow, a raft, and a box painted like a comic strip.

spotlights.name: Sikki grass craft
spotlights.spot_it: Golden grass coiled into boxes, baskets and animals, with stripes of magenta, green and blue.
spotlights.story_md: Sikki is a golden grass that grows in the wet fields of north Bihar. Women cut it, dry it, dye some of it, and coil it tightly over a core of coarser munj grass with a needle-like tool called a takua. The result is light, stiff and shines like straw-gold: lidded boxes (*pauti*) traditionally given to a bride, toys, elephants, figures of gods. It is a craft of the same Mithila households that paint, and like Mithila painting it moved from home use to sale in the late 20th century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Turns a weed of the paddy field into a family heirloom.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold grass, coiled by needle, given with the bride.

spotlights.name: Patna Kalam painting
spotlights.spot_it: Small watercolours of ordinary working people, often against a plain background with no landscape: a glassmaker, a snake charmer, a fishmonger.
spotlights.story_md: When Mughal and Nawabi patronage collapsed in the 18th century, painters from Murshidabad moved to Patna and found new buyers: British officials who wanted pictures of Indian life to send home. The **Patna School** (Patna Kalam) painted what court artists ignored: the bangle-maker, the potter, the snake charmer, the washerman, festivals and markets. Figures were drawn with soft shading and set on plain paper, often in sets of trades. Painters such as Sewak Ram and Shiv Lal led it; Ishwari Prasad Varma, who died in 1950, is called its last master.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first Indian painting school to make ordinary working people its main subject.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the court stopped paying, the painters went to the bazaar.

spotlights.name: Didarganj Yakshi
spotlights.spot_it: A life-size woman in glossy polished sandstone holding a fly-whisk over her shoulder, with heavy anklets and a beaded girdle.
spotlights.story_md: On 18 October 1917, villagers on the Ganga bank at Didarganj in Patna dug out a buried statue. An official letter credits a man named **Ghulam Rasul** with the find; local retellings add a snake that slipped under the stone. She is a **yakshi**, a nature spirit, about 1.6 m tall, holding a chauri (fly-whisk), carved from Chunar sandstone and polished to a shine. Many scholars call her Mauryan, 3rd century BCE; others argue for the 1st or 2nd century CE. She is the star of the Bihar Museum, where she moved in 2017.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Probably the most celebrated piece of ancient Indian sculpture in stone.
spotlights.memory_hook: Found by a river, dated by argument, polished like glass.

spotlights.name: Bismillah Khan
spotlights.spot_it: The sound of the shehnai, a reed pipe, played by a small man in a cap at India's first Independence Day.
spotlights.story_md: Bismillah Khan was born on 21 March 1916 in **Dumraon**, in today's Buxar district, into a family of musicians at the Dumraon court. As a boy he moved to Varanasi to learn from his uncle, and Varanasi became his home. He took the **shehnai**, an instrument of weddings and temple gates, into the concert hall. On the eve of 15 August 1947 he played at the Red Fort. He received the **Bharat Ratna** in 2001. He was offered a life in America and is said to have asked whether they could bring the Ganga too.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The shehnai's place in classical music is largely his doing, and he was born in Bihar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born in Dumraon, married to Varanasi, heard at the Red Fort.

spotlights.name: Sharda Sinha
spotlights.spot_it: A clear, high, folk voice singing Chhath songs from every loudspeaker in October and November.
spotlights.story_md: Sharda Sinha, born in 1952 in Supaul district and known as **Bihar Kokila** (the nightingale of Bihar), sang folk songs in Maithili, Bhojpuri and Magahi for more than 50 years. Her Chhath songs, such as *Ho Deenanath* and *Kelwa ke paat par*, are what Bihar hears every Chhath; for migrants they are the sound of home. Hindi film audiences know her from *Kahe Toh Se Sajna* in *Maine Pyar Kiya* (1989). She died in Delhi on **5 November 2024**, the first day of that year's Chhath. In 2025 she was awarded the **Padma Vibhushan** posthumously.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Her voice is Chhath, and Chhath is Bihar.
spotlights.memory_hook: She died on the first day of the festival she had sung for 50 years.

sections.title: Food: fire, seeds and things that keep
sections.intro_md:
Bihari food is the food of the Ganga plain: rice and wheat, lentils, mustard oil, seasonal greens and a lot of **roasted gram**. Cooking over an open fire matters: litti, chokha and the roasted mashes called chokha or bharta all take their taste from smoke. Mustard oil and panch phoron (five-spice) tie it to Bengal; sattu and the tandoor-free breads tie it to eastern UP.

Many of its best-known foods share one feature: they keep. Sattu, thekua, tilkut, khaja and anarsa all last for days or weeks, which suits a hot climate and a population that has always travelled for work and pilgrimage.

Other names to try: **dal pitthi** (dumplings of dough stuffed with lentils), **kadhi bari**, **dahi chura** on Sankranti, **Champaran mutton** slow-cooked in sealed clay pots called *ahuna* or *handi*, **malpua**, and **khurchan** sweets. Bihar also has a run of GI-tagged products, listed in the table below.

spotlights.name: Litti chokha
spotlights.spot_it: Fist-sized wheat balls roasted over coals until charred, broken open and soaked in ghee, eaten with a smoky mash of brinjal, tomato and potato.
spotlights.story_md: **Litti** is a ball of whole-wheat dough stuffed with **sattu** (roasted gram flour) mixed with garlic, ginger, ajwain, lemon, chilli and mustard oil, ideally roasted over dried cow-dung cakes or coals, then dunked in ghee. **Chokha** is brinjal, tomato and potato roasted in the same fire, peeled and mashed with raw onion, garlic, chilli and mustard oil. It needs no utensils and keeps for a day, which is why it is called the food of travellers and soldiers; the story that 1857 rebels lived on it is folklore. India Post put it on a stamp in 2017.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dish people across India think of when they think of Bihar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fire outside, sattu inside, ghee on top.

spotlights.name: Makhana (fox nut)
spotlights.spot_it: Light, white, puffed seeds the size of a marble, roasted with ghee and salt.
spotlights.story_md: Makhana is the seed of *Euryale ferox*, a water lily with giant prickly leaves that grows in the ponds of Mithila and the Kosi region. Divers, mostly from the **Mallah** fishing community, feel for the seeds in the mud at the bottom. The seeds are dried, roasted in iron pans and struck with wooden mallets so the kernel pops out white. A government reply in Parliament put Bihar's share of India's output at about **85%**, and India grows about 80% of the world's. 'Mithila Makhana' got a GI tag in 2022, and a **National Makhana Board** was launched at Purnea in September 2025.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A pond crop of the poorest villages became a global health snack.
spotlights.memory_hook: A diver in the mud, a hammer on a pan, a snack in a gym bag.

spotlights.name: Shahi litchi of Muzaffarpur
spotlights.spot_it: Red, rough-skinned fruit sold in bunches with leaves, for about three weeks in May and June.
spotlights.story_md: Muzaffarpur's **Shahi litchi**, with its rose scent and small seed, got a GI tag in 2018, and Bihar is India's largest litchi grower. For years the season also brought outbreaks of a deadly brain illness among small children in the district. A 2017 study in *The Lancet Global Health* by Indian and US scientists linked it to children eating litchis all day and skipping the evening meal: unripe litchis contain **hypoglycin A and MCPG**, which block the body's ability to make sugar overnight. The advice was simple: limit litchis, never skip dinner, and treat low blood sugar fast.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A beloved fruit and a public-health lesson in the same orchard.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eat your litchis, then eat your dinner.

spotlights.name: Khaja of Silao
spotlights.spot_it: A rectangular pastry of many thin crisp layers, soaked lightly in syrup.
spotlights.story_md: Silao, a small town between Rajgir and Nalanda, is known for **khaja**: wheat dough rolled into many fine layers, fried and dipped in sugar syrup so it shatters when you bite it. Local sellers like to say it has 52 layers. Every bus between Rajgir and Nalanda stops so passengers can buy boxes, and Silao khaja received a **GI tag** in 2018. Similar layered khaja is made in Odisha (for Puri's Jagannath temple) and Andhra, but Silao's is the Bihar version.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A roadside sweet with a legal geographical identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Count the layers before it breaks.

sections.title: Festivals: the sun, a fair and the sisters
sections.intro_md:
Bihar celebrates the all-India festivals, Holi (called Phaguwa), Diwali, Durga Puja, Eid, Muharram, but its own calendar is built around rivers and the sun.

The year's centre is **Chhath** in October or November. Then come **Sama Chakeva** in Mithila and the **Sonepur Mela** from the Kartik full moon. In January **Makar Sankranti** brings dahi chura and tilkut. In March to April there is a second, Chaiti Chhath. In the monsoon month of Shravan, hundreds of thousands of *kanwariyas* in saffron collect Ganga water at **Sultanganj** and walk barefoot about 105 km to the Shiva temple at Deoghar in Jharkhand. In August Bhagalpur worships the snake goddess with Manjusha boxes. In September **Pitru Paksha** fills Gaya with pilgrims making offerings for the dead.

The ring below shows the year at a glance.

data.name: Makar Sankranti: dahi chura and tilkut

spotlights.name: Chhath
spotlights.spot_it: Women standing waist-deep in a river at sunset and sunrise, holding up bamboo trays of fruit and thekua to the sun, with songs from every bank.
spotlights.story_md: Chhath worships **Surya**, the sun, and **Chhathi Maiya**, over four days six days after Diwali. Day one, *nahay khay*: a bath and a pure meal. Day two, *kharna*: a fast all day, broken at night with jaggery kheer, then a fast without even water for about 36 hours. Day three: families walk to a river or pond and the vrati, usually a woman, offers *arghya* to the **setting** sun. Day four: the same to the rising sun, and the fast ends. There is no priest, no idol and no temple; the family does everything. Patna alone prepares more than 100 ghats. A second, smaller Chhath falls in March or April.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bihar's biggest festival, and the one that pulls migrants home from across India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The only big festival that bows to the setting sun.

spotlights.name: Sonepur Mela
spotlights.spot_it: A month-long fair on the sandbanks where the Gandak meets the Ganga, with horses, cattle, circuses and theatre tents.
spotlights.story_md: From **Kartik Purnima** (the full moon of October or November) a huge fair grows at Sonepur, at the meeting of the Gandak and the Ganga, by the Harihar Nath temple. Legend sets the battle of an elephant and a crocodile here, ended by Vishnu. For centuries it was billed as Asia's largest cattle fair, famous for **elephants** sold by landowners and temples. Elephant sales are now banned under wildlife law, and the last elephants stopped coming after the mid-2010s; rules on cattle sales in 2017 hit the trade further. Today the mela is horses, dogs, birds, handicrafts, food, circus and theatre.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how an ancient trading fair changes when law and economy change.
spotlights.memory_hook: Once you could buy an elephant here; now you buy a balloon.

spotlights.name: Sama Chakeva
spotlights.spot_it: Sisters carrying trays of painted clay birds and figures, singing at night across the fields of Mithila.
spotlights.story_md: Sama Chakeva is a festival of **brothers and sisters** in Mithila, held in the weeks after Chhath until the Kartik full moon, when birds from the Himalaya arrive in the plains. Sisters make clay figures: **Sama**, a daughter of Krishna who was turned into a bird after a false accusation, her loyal brother **Chakeva**, and **Chugla**, the tell-tale who lied about her. Each night they sing over the figures and set fire to Chugla's moustache. On the full moon the figures are immersed or broken in the fields and the brothers are blessed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A festival made by girls and women, with its own clay art.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every year Mithila's sisters burn the gossip's moustache.

sections.title: How Bihar lives
sections.intro_md:
Bihar is young, rural and on the move. Nearly nine in ten people live in villages. Fertility, at 3.0 children per woman in 2019 to 2021, is falling but still the highest of any large state, so the median Bihari is a teenager or young adult.

**Migration** is the central experience. The Economic Survey of 2016 to 2017 found Bihar and Uttar Pradesh to be the biggest sources of people moving between states. Their remittances keep many villages going, and the 2020 lockdown walk home made them visible to the whole country.

**Caste** shapes politics, marriage and land, and since 2023 the state has numbers for it (see the chart). **Women** got 50% of panchayat seats in 2006, bicycles for school, and self-help groups. Alcohol has been banned since **April 2016**; supporters credit it with less domestic violence, critics point to smuggling, hundreds of thousands of arrests and deaths from illicit liquor. Education is a deep hunger: Patna's coaching classes, Anand Kumar's Super 30 and the civil service exam are roads out for many families.

spotlights.name: The 2023 caste survey
spotlights.spot_it: A government enumerator with a form at the door, asking every household its caste.
spotlights.story_md: India's census has not counted castes (except SC and ST) since 1931. In 2023 Bihar did it itself. Released on 2 October 2023, the survey counted **13.07 crore** people: **Extremely Backward Classes 36.01%**, Other Backward Classes 27.12%, Scheduled Castes 19.65%, Scheduled Tribes 1.68%, and the unreserved 15.52%. The **Yadavs**, at 14.26%, were the largest single caste. Bihar then raised its caste quotas to 65%, but the Patna High Court struck that down on 20 June 2024. In April 2025 the central government announced that the next national census would count caste, a decision Bihar's survey helped force.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first full caste count anywhere in India in nearly a century.
spotlights.memory_hook: 36% EBC: the biggest group was the one politics talked about least.

spotlights.name: Bicycles for schoolgirls
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of girls in school uniform cycling down a village road together.
spotlights.story_md: In 2006 Bihar began giving every girl who enrolled in Class 9 money to buy a **bicycle**. The idea was simple: secondary schools are far from many villages, and walking alone was slow and felt unsafe. Economists **Karthik Muralidharan and Nishith Prakash** studied the results, comparing girls with boys and with Jharkhand. They found the scheme raised girls' age-appropriate secondary school enrolment by **32%** and cut the gender gap by 40%, mostly in villages far from a school, and at lower cost than cash transfers. The sight of girls cycling in groups became a symbol of the change.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A cheap, physical fix that changed girls' schooling, and a famous case in development economics.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bicycle beat a cash transfer.

spotlights.name: Jeevika didis
spotlights.spot_it: Women in bright saris at a village meeting, passbooks in hand: the self-help groups of Jeevika.
spotlights.story_md: **Jeevika**, Bihar's rural livelihoods programme, began in 2006 to 2007 with World Bank support. It organises village women into self-help groups of 10 to 15 members who save small amounts weekly, lend to each other and then borrow from banks. Members are called **Jeevika didis**, and their numbers run into crores. They run canteens in hospitals, sell goods, and have become a political force. In September 2025 the state's **Mukhyamantri Mahila Rozgar Yojana** paid ₹10,000 each to 75 lakh women through this network; another 25 lakh received payments in February 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest organised network of rural women in Bihar, and now a key voting bloc.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten women, a passbook, and a vote.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
History made Bihar's best-known people: Ashoka, Chanakya, Aryabhata, the Buddha's patrons Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, Sher Shah, Guru Gobind Singh, Kunwar Singh, JP. You met them above.

This section is the modern era: **politics** as a contest of caste and dignity (Karpoori Thakur, Lalu Prasad, Nitish Kumar), **grit** against a state that often failed (Dashrath Manjhi), and **talent that leaves**: actors such as Pankaj Tripathi and Manoj Bajpayee in Mumbai, musicians in Varanasi.

Others worth a search: the poet **Ramdhari Singh Dinkar** and novelist **Phanishwar Nath Renu**; **Bindeshwar Pathak** of Vaishali, who founded Sulabh and its pay-and-use toilets; the mathematician **Vashishtha Narayan Singh**; and, newest, cricketer **Vaibhav Suryavanshi** of Samastipur, who in April 2025 hit an IPL hundred off 35 balls at the age of 14.

spotlights.name: Rajendra Prasad
spotlights.spot_it: A grey-moustached man in a white Gandhi cap: India's first President.
spotlights.story_md: Rajendra Prasad was born in 1884 at **Ziradei** in Siwan district and topped the Calcutta University entrance exam. A popular story says an examiner wrote on his answer sheet that "the examinee is better than the examiner"; it is a legend that cannot be checked. He gave up a big law practice to work with Gandhi at **Champaran** in 1917, presided over the Constituent Assembly, and became **India's first President** in 1950. He is the only person elected to the office twice, serving until 1962. He spent his last months at Sadaqat Ashram in Patna.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bihar gave the Republic its first head of state.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Ziradei to Rashtrapati Bhavan, twice.

spotlights.name: Karpoori Thakur
spotlights.spot_it: A thin man in a crumpled kurta; a statue of him is garlanded on every 24 January.
spotlights.story_md: Karpoori Thakur (1924 to 1988), from the barber (Nai) caste, one of Bihar's extremely backward castes, was chief minister twice. As education minister he dropped English as a compulsory pass subject for the school-leaving exam. As chief minister in 1978 he brought in reservation in state jobs that set aside a separate quota for the **most backward castes**, plus quotas for women and poor upper castes: the 'Karpoori formula'. He was famous for living poor: no house of his own, a borrowed coat for foreign travel. He was awarded the **Bharat Ratna** posthumously in 2024, his birth centenary.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His formula of a separate quota for the poorest castes still shapes Bihar's politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Jan Nayak: the chief minister who borrowed a coat.

spotlights.name: Dashrath Manjhi
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow road through a cleft in a rocky hill near Gaya, cut by one man with a hammer and chisel.
spotlights.story_md: Dashrath Manjhi was a landless labourer of the **Musahar** community in Gehlaur, a village cut off by a rocky ridge. After his wife Falguni Devi was hurt crossing the hill and died without reaching care in time, he began, around 1960, to cut a path through it with a **hammer and chisel**. He worked for **22 years**, until 1982, and made a passage about 110 m long and 9 m wide. It cut the trip from Atri to Wazirganj from about 55 km to 15 km. Villagers called him mad, then the Mountain Man. He died in 2007; a 2015 film told his story.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof of what one person could do, and of what the state had failed to do.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-two years, one hammer, one hill.

spotlights.name: Lalu Prasad Yadav
spotlights.spot_it: A man with a grin and a quick earthy one-liner, who ran Bihar from 1990 and then the Indian Railways.
spotlights.story_md: Lalu Prasad came out of the JP movement and became chief minister in 1990. For backward castes and Muslims he was the first leader who spoke like them and gave them **voice and dignity**; in October 1990 he had L. K. Advani arrested at Samastipur and stopped the Ram rath yatra. For critics his rule (with his wife **Rabri Devi** as chief minister from 1997 to 2005) meant collapsing roads, kidnapping and 'jungle raj'. He was convicted in the **fodder scam** cases from 2013. As railway minister (2004 to 2009) he claimed a famous financial turnaround. His son **Tejashwi Yadav** leads the RJD.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He changed who held power in Bihar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Social justice and jungle raj: same man, different listeners.

spotlights.name: Nitish Kumar
spotlights.spot_it: A quiet engineer in a white kurta who was sworn in as chief minister a record ten times.
spotlights.story_md: Nitish Kumar, born in 1951 at Bakhtiyarpur and trained as an electrical engineer, was another JP student activist. He became chief minister in November 2005 and, apart from short breaks, held the job for about **20 years**, switching between the BJP-led NDA and its opponents several times. His record: roads, power, policing, **bicycles for schoolgirls**, 50% panchayat seats for women, prohibition and the caste survey. Supporters called him 'Sushasan Babu' (Mr Good Governance). He took oath for a record **10th time** on 20 November 2025, then resigned on 14 April 2026 to move to the Rajya Sabha.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The longest-serving chief minister in Bihar's history.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten oaths, two alliances, one bicycle.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
A first trip to Bihar is usually the **Buddhist circuit**: Bodh Gaya, Rajgir, Nalanda, Vaishali, Kesariya, and on to Kushinagar in UP where the Buddha died. Winter (November to February) is the season; summer on the plain is fierce and the monsoon floods the north.

Patna has the **Bihar Museum**, Golghar, Takht Sri Patna Sahib, Kumhrar, and the Ganga ghats at Chhath. In the southwest are Sasaram's tomb, Rohtasgarh and the Kaimur waterfalls. In the north, Madhubani's painted villages and Valmiki's forest. In the east, Bhagalpur's silk looms and the dolphin sanctuary, and Vikramashila.

spotlights.name: Bihar Museum
spotlights.spot_it: A long low building of rust-coloured metal panels and courtyards on Bailey Road, Patna.
spotlights.story_md: Opened in 2015, the Bihar Museum was designed by the Japanese firm of **Fumihiko Maki** with the Mumbai practice Opolis as a campus of low pavilions and courtyards rather than one block. Its history galleries run from prehistory to the Mauryas, Guptas and Palas, and its star exhibit is the **Didarganj Yakshi**, moved here from the old Patna Museum in 2017. It also has a children's museum and hosts a museum biennale. It is the best single place to see why the first half of this day matters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bihar's ancient past, in one modern building.
spotlights.memory_hook: Go for the Yakshi, stay for the Mauryas.

spotlights.name: Vishwa Shanti Stupa, Rajgir
spotlights.spot_it: A white dome with four golden Buddhas on top of Ratnagiri hill, reached by single-seat chairlift.
spotlights.story_md: The Japanese monk **Nichidatsu Fujii** and his order, Nipponzan Myohoji, built peace pagodas around the world after Hiroshima. Rajgir's, on Ratnagiri hill, was completed in **1969**, one of the first. Its four golden statues show the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, first sermon and death. You reach it by an aerial ropeway of single open chairs, also from 1969, and a newer cabin ropeway. From the top you see the five hills of old Rajagriha and Vulture's Peak, where the Buddha taught. Rajgir also has hot springs, a nature safari with a glass skywalk, and Ghora Katora lake.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The easiest way to see Rajgir's hills from above.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Japanese peace pagoda over Magadha's first capital.

sections.title: How Bihar earns
sections.intro_md:
Bihar's economy is the size of a mid-sized country's, about **₹9.92 lakh crore** in 2024-25, but it is shared among about 13 crore people. Income per person at current prices was about **₹76,490**, and the state's own survey put per capita income at roughly a third (31.7%) of the all-India average, the lowest of any state.

The gap is old: colonial land rules, then the **freight equalisation** policy (1952 to 1993), which removed the advantage of factories near south Bihar's mines. In 2000 the mines went to **Jharkhand** anyway.

What Bihar has: fertile land and water (it leads India in makhana and litchi and has a growing maize belt in the Kosi districts), a vast young workforce, and money sent home by migrants. Industry is thin: the Barauni refinery and fertiliser plants, sugar mills, food processing.

Growth has been faster than India's for three years running (chart). The challenge is turning it into jobs at home.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Bihar attracts stereotypes, and some flattering myths too. A few to sort out:

- **"Bihar means land of monasteries."** Fact, more or less. The name comes from *vihara*, Buddhist monastery, probably from the many viharas around Bihar Sharif and Nalanda.
- **"India's national emblem comes from Bihar."** Myth. The four-lion capital is from Sarnath in UP. Bihar's Ashokan pillars at Vaishali and Lauriya Nandangarh carry a single lion.
- **"Nalanda's library burned for three months."** Unproven. The story comes from much later accounts. A Tibetan visitor in the 1230s found monks still teaching there.
- **"Nalanda was the world's first university."** Half true: it was a monastic centre of learning, and Taxila was older.
- **"Chhath is only for Biharis."** Myth. It is equally central in eastern UP, Jharkhand and Nepal's Terai, and is celebrated wherever their migrants live.
- **"Litti chokha fed the 1857 rebels."** Folklore. Nice story, no source.
- **"Bihar is poor because Bihari people do not work."** False. Biharis are among India's most mobile workers. Poverty here has structural causes: land, floods, policy and the loss of the minerals in 2000.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Dated items, most recent first:

- **15 April 2026**: Samrat Choudhary sworn in as the first BJP chief minister, a day after Nitish Kumar resigned to go to the Rajya Sabha.
- **16 February 2026**: ₹10,000 each paid to another 25 lakh women under the Mahila Rozgar Yojana.
- **2 February 2026**: The Economic Survey 2025-26 reports growth of 13.1% at current prices in 2024-25, above India's 9.8%.
- **20 November 2025**: Nitish Kumar takes oath for a record 10th time.
- **14 November 2025**: NDA wins 202 of 243 seats; turnout 67.13%.
- **6 October 2025**: Patna Metro's first section opens.
- **26 September 2025**: ₹10,000 each paid to 75 lakh women, the first round of the Mahila Rozgar Yojana.
- **15 September 2025**: National Makhana Board launched at Purnea.
- **30 September 2025**: Final voter roll after the Special Intensive Revision: 7.42 crore electors.

spotlights.name: The 2025 election and the voter roll
spotlights.spot_it: Long queues of women outside polling booths, and a fight over who was on the list.
spotlights.story_md: Before the vote, the Election Commission ran a **Special Intensive Revision** of Bihar's electoral roll from 24 June 2025. The final roll, published on 30 September, had **7.42 crore** electors, down from 7.89 crore: about 68.7 lakh names deleted (for deaths, migration and duplicates) and 21.5 lakh added. The opposition said genuine voters were struck off; the Commission defended it. Polling was on 6 and 11 November; turnout was **67.13%**, reported as the highest since 1951. Results on 14 November gave the NDA **202 of 243 seats** (BJP 89, JD(U) 85). Prashant Kishor's new Jan Suraaj party contested widely and made little impact.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The election that set up Bihar's first BJP chief minister.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fewer names on the roll, more people at the booth.

spotlights.name: Samrat Choudhary, first BJP chief minister
spotlights.spot_it: A politician in a saffron turban taking the oath in Patna in April 2026.
spotlights.story_md: After the 2025 win, Nitish Kumar was sworn in for the 10th time on 20 November 2025. On **14 April 2026** he resigned to enter the Rajya Sabha, ending about 20 years as chief minister. The next day, **15 April 2026**, Samrat Choudhary, a Kushwaha (Koeri) leader and former deputy chief minister, was sworn in as Bihar's 24th chief minister: the **first from the BJP** in the state. JD(U) leaders Vijay Kumar Chaudhary and Bijendra Prasad Yadav became deputy chief ministers. For the first time the BJP, rather than a regional party, leads Bihar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ends the Lalu and Nitish era that began in 1990.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirty-five years of JP's students, then a new name.

spotlights.name: Patna Metro
spotlights.spot_it: A blue and white train on an elevated track past Patna's bus terminal.
spotlights.story_md: Patna's first metro section opened on **6 October 2025**, hours before the election schedule was announced, with passenger service from the next day. The first stretch of the Blue Line runs from the Patliputra Bus Terminal (ISBT) through Zero Mile to Bhoothnath; fares are ₹15 to ₹30 and trains came every 20 minutes at first. The whole project, started in 2019, is estimated at about ₹13,365 crore. Underground sections toward Patna Junction and Rajendra Nagar are being tunnelled for the next phase.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small start, but the first metro in one of India's largest and least urban states.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two thousand years after Pataliputra's 64 gates, Patna gets a metro.

sections.title: Recap: Bihar in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. **Name**: from *vihara*, monastery. Capital Patna, once Pataliputra.
2. **Land**: the Ganga splits a flood-prone north (Mithila, Champaran, Kosi) from a drier south (Magadh). The Kosi moves; the dolphins stay.
3. **Empire**: Magadha, Mauryas and Guptas ruled India from here. Ashoka was born in Patna; Aryabhata worked there.
4. **Learning**: Nalanda and Vikramashila drew Asia's scholars until about 1200.
5. **Faiths**: Bodh Gaya (Buddhism), Pawapuri and Vaishali (Jainism), Gaya (rites for the dead), Patna Sahib (Sikhism), Maner (Sufism).
6. **Arts**: Mithila painting, Manjusha, sikki, the Didarganj Yakshi, Bismillah Khan, Sharda Sinha.
7. **Food**: litti chokha, sattu, makhana (85% of India's), Shahi litchi, tilkut, khaja, thekua.
8. **Festival**: Chhath, no priest, no idol, offerings to the setting and rising sun.
9. **Society**: young, rural, migrant; caste counted in 2023; prohibition since 2016.
10. **Now**: NDA's 202 seats in 2025; Samrat Choudhary, first BJP chief minister, April 2026.

best_facts.fact: The rupee began in Bihar's neighbourhood: Sher Shah Suri of Sasaram issued a silver coin of about 178 grains called the rupiya in the 1540s, after driving the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India.
best_facts.why_surprising: A currency used by over a billion people traces back to a five-year reign from a small Bihar town.

best_facts.fact: Workers in Ashoka's time polished the inside of granite caves in the Barabar Hills so smoothly that they still reflect light 2,250 years later. E. M. Forster turned them into the Marabar Caves of A Passage to India.
best_facts.why_surprising: Mirror-polished granite, 2,250 years old, with a cameo in English literature.

best_facts.fact: Litchis plus a skipped dinner explained a deadly yearly brain illness in Muzaffarpur's children: toxins in unripe fruit block sugar production overnight (Lancet Global Health, 2017).

best_facts.fact: The Kosi wandered about 120 km west across north Bihar over roughly 250 years; in 2008 it broke its embankment and jumped about 120 km back east in days.

best_facts.fact: Giving schoolgirls bicycles raised their secondary enrolment by 32% in Bihar, at lower cost than cash transfers, according to a study published in 2017.

best_facts.why_surprising: One man did what the state would not.

best_facts.fact: Mithila painting was almost unknown outside village homes until the 1934 earthquake knocked down walls and a British officer, William Archer, photographed the murals inside.
best_facts.why_surprising: A disaster revealed one of India's best-known arts.

best_facts.fact: Bihar grows about 85% of India's makhana, and India grows about 80% of the world's: most of the planet's fox nuts are dived out of ponds in a few districts of Mithila.
best_facts.why_surprising: A global 'superfood' comes from one small region's ponds.

best_facts.fact: Aryabhata, working at Kusumapura (Patna), wrote in 499 CE, aged 23, that the earth rotates on its axis, and gave pi as 3.1416.
best_facts.why_surprising: Over a thousand years before Copernicus, from Patna.

best_facts.fact: Bismillah Khan, the shehnai player most associated with Varanasi, was born at Dumraon in Bihar in 1916.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most people assume he was from Banaras.

best_facts.fact: Vaishali's Vajji league was governed by an assembly of clan heads around 500 BCE, one of the earliest known republics anywhere.
best_facts.why_surprising: Republics are usually credited to Athens and Rome.

best_facts.fact: Chhath has no priest, no idol and no temple ritual: the family itself makes the offerings, and the most crowded moment is the offering to the setting sun.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most festivals hail the rising sun and need a priest.

best_facts.fact: In Bihar's 2023 caste survey, the largest group was the Extremely Backward Classes at 36%, larger than the better-known OBCs at 27%.
best_facts.why_surprising: The biggest bloc was the least discussed.

best_facts.fact: Rabindranath Tagore's first pen-name, Bhanusimha, was used for teenage poems imitating Vidyapati, a 14th to 15th century Maithili poet from Bihar.
best_facts.why_surprising: Bengal's greatest poet began by copying a Bihari one.

best_facts.fact: Vaibhav Suryavanshi of Samastipur hit an IPL hundred off 35 balls on 28 April 2025, aged 14 years and 32 days, the youngest IPL centurion.
Golghar, Patna's giant granary of 1786, was built to hold about 140,000 tonnes of grain and was never filled.
best_facts.why_surprising: A famine-proof granary that never held a full harvest.

best_facts.fact: Nitish Kumar was sworn in as chief minister a record ten times, and both he and his long-time rival Lalu Prasad began as student activists in JP's 1974 movement.
best_facts.why_surprising: Bihar's two great rivals came from the same protest.

side_dish.title: The Ajivikas: India's lost school of fate
side_dish.body_md:
The Barabar caves were not cut for Buddhists or Jains. Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha gave them to the **Ajivikas**, a group of wandering ascetics who were, for a few centuries, as important as both.

Their teacher, **Makkhali Gosala**, was a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira, and for a while a companion of Mahavira. His big idea was **niyati**: destiny. Everything that happens to every being is fixed in advance, like a ball of thread that unwinds to its full length and then stops. Good deeds do not speed up liberation and bad deeds do not delay it. Every soul passes through a set number of lives, about 8.4 million great cycles in their reckoning, and then is freed.

That sounds like an argument for doing nothing, but Ajivikas lived hard, naked, ascetic lives. Scholars still argue about why: perhaps because their discipline was itself part of what was fated.

We know them mostly through their enemies. Not one Ajivika text survives; Buddhist and Jain books describe them, usually to attack them. The sect faded after the Mauryas, though inscriptions in south India mention Ajivikas as late as the 14th century.

Next time you hear someone say "it was meant to be", you are close to Gosala. The difference is that he believed it about everything, and built a way of life on it.

offline_task.title: Make sattu sharbat (two glasses, five minutes)
offline_task.body_md:
**Sattu** is roasted chickpea flour. Look for it in any Indian grocery labelled "chana sattu"; it is beige and smells toasted.

**You need**
- 4 tablespoons sattu
- 2 glasses cold water
- Juice of 1 lemon
- ½ teaspoon roasted cumin powder
- Black salt (kala namak) and plain salt to taste
- 1 small onion, very finely chopped
- 1 green chilli, finely chopped (optional)
- A few mint or coriander leaves

**Steps**
1. Put the sattu in a jug and add half a glass of water. Whisk with a fork until there are no lumps, like a thin batter.
2. Add the rest of the water, the lemon juice, cumin, black salt and salt. Stir hard.
3. Stir in the onion, chilli and herbs.
4. Pour into two glasses. Stir again just before drinking, because sattu settles.

**Sweet version**: skip onion, chilli and salt; add jaggery or sugar and a pinch of cardamom.

**Notice**: this is what farm workers across the Ganga plain drink at noon in May. It fills you up for hours on a few rupees. That is the point.
